Listen to this article Share The federal government has said the groundbreaking of the long-awaited upgrade of the ageing Apapa and Tin Can Island ports in Lagos will begin on November 25. “Adegboyega Oyetola, the minister of Marine and Blue Economy, will on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, perform the groundbreaking ceremony and official turning of the soil for the comprehensive modernisation and upgrade of the Lagos Port Complex, Apapa, and the Tin-Can Island Port Complex, Lagos,” the ministry’s spokesperson wrote in a statement on Monday. The announcement came on the same day BusinessDay published a report highlighting the worsening operational challenges facing traders and port operators as deteriorating infrastructure at the two ports remains largely unaddressed, despite a £746 million (N1.3 trillion) financing agreement with the United Kingdom signed in March. Read also: Nigeria’s ageing Apapa, Tin Can ports struggle as N1.3trn reconstruction stalls According to people at the Nigeria Ports Authority (NPA) familiar with the matter, the Nigerian government was to fulfil counterpart funding commitments before the project could fully move into its construction phase. The first phase had only recently received Federal Executive Council approval for disbursement by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). The source did not disclose the amount. Commissioned in 1926, Apapa port is nearly a century old, while Tin Can Island port began operations in 1977. Both remain critical to Nigeria’s maritime trade, largely because of their proximity to the country’s commercial centre, despite years of neglect. The dilapidation has led to longer vessel turnaround times, longer cargo dwell times, lesser ship calls and lower cargo throughput are weakening their competitiveness against better-equipped regional ports. Read also: Nigerian ports record slower vessel turnaround in H1 2026 At Apapa, vessel turnaround time increased from 5.9 days to 6.1 days in the first half of 2026, according to Nigeria Ports Authority (NPA) figures, as opposed to regional ports like Tema in Ghana averaging three to four days. At Tin Can, vessel calls fell 3.4 percent to 488 from 505 in the first half of 2025, while turnaround time increased from 4.4 days to 5.1 days. Together, the two ports handle more than 85 percent of Nigeria’s container trade, according to the NBS. “Their modernisation is therefore critical to expanding trade capacity, facilitating exports, improving cargo delivery and consolidating Nigeria’s position as a major maritime and commercial hub in West and Central Africa,” the ministry said. Construction documents by ITB Nigeria, the contractor engaged for the works and obtained by BusinessDay, detail plans to rehabilitate bollards, safety ladders and apron slabs, alongside structural works to support modern ship-to-shore gantry cranes. It is also expected to improve berthing and cargo-handling capacity, reduce vessel turnaround and cargo dwell times, and lower demurrage and logistics costs for importers and exporters. “The project…will provide an opportunity to transform the ports into more efficient, technologically advanced and commercially competitive facilities capable of responding to the changing dynamics of global shipping and international trade,” the ministry said. The UK-financing agreement, facilitated by Citibank, includes substantial procurement commitments to British companies. At least £236 million in supplier contracts is expected to go to UK firms, including a £70 million contract for British Steel to supply 120,000 tonnes of steel billets for the reconstruction. Read also: FG secures £746m facility to modernise Apapa, Tin-Can ports The British Steel order is the company’s largest export contract backed by UK Export Finance.
